questions.stem: Where is The Memory Police set?
options: In Tokyo during the Second World War, under strict military rule
In a mountain village in Japan that is cut off by an avalanche
In an unnamed city on the Japanese mainland, under military rule
On an unnamed island where things and memories of them disappear
questions.explanation: The novel takes place on an unnamed island. Objects and ideas vanish one by one, and the Memory Police make sure nobody keeps them.

questions.stem: What happens to the islanders when something 'disappears'?
options: The Memory Police remove the object, and the islanders mourn its loss
They lose their memories and feelings about it, then get rid of it
The object vanishes overnight, but everyone still remembers it
They keep the object, but its name is erased from their language
questions.explanation: A disappearance starts in the mind: people wake up and can no longer connect with the thing. They then burn it, bury it or throw it in the river.

questions.stem: What is the narrator's work at the start of the novel?
options: She is a novelist who has published several books
She is an editor who prepares other writers' novels for print
She is a sculptor who carries on her late mother's work
She is a teacher at the island's only remaining school
questions.explanation: The narrator writes novels, and R is her editor. Her writing becomes important when even novels begin to disappear.

questions.stem: Why is the narrator's editor, R, in danger?
options: He refused to burn the island's library when he was ordered to
He cannot forget, and the Memory Police hunt people like him
He has published a book that criticises the Memory Police by name
He has been caught smuggling islanders off the island by boat
questions.explanation: R keeps his memories when others lose theirs. The Memory Police take away people like him, so he must hide.

questions.stem: Where does the narrator hide R?
options: In her mother's old studio, behind a tall cabinet full of sculptures
In a cave in the hills beyond the observatory above the town
In a secret room built beneath the floor of her father's old study
On the abandoned ferry where the old man lives by the harbour
questions.explanation: The narrator and the old man build a hidden room under the floor of her late father's study. R lives there, unseen, for the rest of the novel.

questions.stem: What does R leave behind when he goes into hiding?
options: His work as a novelist, which he must give up
His elderly father, who lives on the old ferry
His wife, who is expecting their child
His mother, who is dying in the hospital
questions.explanation: R's wife is pregnant, but he must disappear from his own life to stay safe. Hiding protects him and costs him his family.

questions.stem: When calendars disappear, what happens to the weather?
options: Winter never ends, and the snow keeps falling
Summer never ends, and the island runs dry
The seasons change every day without warning
Rain falls without stopping until the river floods
questions.explanation: Once calendars are gone, time seems to stop moving forward and the island is stuck in winter. The endless snow becomes a picture of a society frozen in place.

questions.stem: When roses disappear, how does nature take part?
options: The rose bushes are dug up by the Memory Police overnight
The roses keep blooming, but nobody can see their colour
The bees that visit roses leave the island the same day
The petals fall from every rose on the island at once
questions.explanation: The disappearances are not only in people's minds: nature follows the same rule, and the petals come away. The image is beautiful and unsettling at once.

questions.stem: What happens when novels disappear?
options: The narrator writes a new novel to replace each one that is lost
Books are burned, and the narrator burns most of hers despite R
The narrator hides her own novels in R's secret room to save them
R is arrested for refusing to give up his collection of novels
questions.explanation: Novels vanish from the islanders' minds and books are burned. R begs the narrator to keep hers and to go on writing, but she can no longer feel what novels were.

questions.stem: Once novels have disappeared, what work does the narrator take up?
options: She becomes a guard
She becomes a typist
She becomes a nurse
She becomes a baker
questions.explanation: With novels gone she works as a typist, yet R persuades her to keep writing her own manuscript in secret.

questions.stem: When some of her mother's sculptures break, what is found inside them?
options: Objects that had been disappeared, which her mother hid away
Letters from her father explaining the Memory Police's plans
Maps showing a secret route off the island to the mainland
Lists naming every islander who could still remember things
questions.explanation: Her mother hid forbidden objects inside her work. The discovery shows how she quietly resisted the disappearances.

questions.stem: Which disappearance comes late in the novel and changes everything?
options: The island's birds, which fly out to sea
The island's roses, whose petals drop off
Parts of the body, beginning with left legs
The island's ferry, which stops for good
questions.explanation: Late in the novel people lose their left legs, then more of their bodies. Forgetting has moved from things people own to the people themselves.

questions.stem: What is ironic about the novel's ending?
options: The old man reveals that he was a member of the Memory Police
R, who hid to survive, walks out of the room after the others vanish
The narrator escapes the island just as the Memory Police find R
The narrator, who hid R, is taken by the Memory Police at the end
questions.explanation: R has been confined while the islanders moved freely. At the end the forgetters, including the narrator, fade away entirely, and the man who remembered steps out of hiding.

questions.stem: What happened to the narrator's mother?
options: She joined the Memory Police and turned against her family
She lost all her memories and forgot she had a daughter
The Memory Police summoned her, and she died soon after
She fled the island by boat and was never heard from again
questions.explanation: Her mother was one of the people who could not forget, and she kept hidden objects. The Memory Police took her away, and she died a week later.

questions.stem: What was the narrator's father's work?
options: He was a sculptor, who shared a studio with his wife
He was a novelist, whose books were burned after his death
He was an ornithologist, who studied birds
He was a ferry worker, who crossed to the mainland
questions.explanation: Her father studied birds. When birds disappear, the Memory Police clear everything to do with birds from his study, erasing his life's work.

questions.stem: Who is the old man?
options: R's father, who has come to the island to look for his son
A family friend who once worked on the ferry and helps hide R
The narrator's uncle, who also cannot forget and hides alongside R
A retired officer of the Memory Police who regrets his work
questions.explanation: The old man is a loyal family friend who used to work on the ferry and lives on it after ferries disappear. He helps build the secret room and looks after the narrator.

questions.stem: How does R try to help the narrator?
options: He plans an escape that will take them both off the island
He shows her lost objects, hoping to bring back her memories
He urges her to report him, so that she will be safe from the police
He writes her novels for her while she works as a typist
questions.explanation: R brings out disappeared objects, such as a music box and a harmonica, and tries to help her feel what they meant. It mostly fails, which shows how complete the forgetting is.

questions.stem: How does the narrator respond to the disappearances, compared with R?
options: She blames R for each loss, while he blames the Memory Police
She mostly accepts each loss, while R fights to keep memory alive
She leads a secret resistance, while R gives up hope in his room
She remembers everything, while R slowly forgets who he is
questions.explanation: The narrator protects R at great risk, but she cannot resist forgetting. Her calm acceptance contrasts with R's struggle, and that contrast drives the novel.

questions.stem: How does Ogawa present the Memory Police?
options: As efficient officers who raid homes and remove anyone who remembers
As distant officials who issue orders but rarely enter people's homes
As clumsy, comic figures whom the islanders easily fool and mock
As open authorities who explain the purpose of each disappearance
questions.explanation: The Memory Police search houses, take people away and remove forbidden things with cold efficiency. They never explain themselves, which makes them more frightening.

questions.stem: The narrator's own manuscript tells of a typist who loses her voice. What happens to her?
options: She joins the Memory Police and helps them find people in hiding
She recovers her voice by reading aloud from her favourite novel
Her typing teacher locks her in a clock tower full of typewriters
She escapes the island and becomes a famous writer on the mainland
questions.explanation: The story within the novel follows a typist trapped by her teacher, who has locked her voice inside a typewriter. Her loss of voice and freedom echoes the island's loss of memory.

questions.stem: How does the typist's story connect with the main plot?
options: It is the novel R wrote before he went into hiding in the secret room
It explains how the narrator's mother hid objects inside her sculptures
Her lost voice and confinement mirror R's hiding and the island's losses
It is a true account of how the Memory Police first came to the island
questions.explanation: The typist is shut away and slowly loses herself, like R in his room and like the islanders losing their memories and bodies. The inner story lets the narrator express what she cannot say directly.

questions.stem: When was The Memory Police first published, and how do English readers know it?
options: In the United States in 1994, then translated into Japanese in 2019
In Japan in 1994, translated into English by Stephen Snyder in 2019
In Britain in 1949, the same year as Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four
In Japan in 2019, translated into English by Yoko Ogawa herself
questions.explanation: Ogawa wrote the novel in Japanese in 1994. Stephen Snyder's English translation appeared in 2019 and brought it a large new readership.

questions.stem: Ogawa has said that one book shaped her as a writer and inspired the secret room. Which book?
options: Fahrenheit 451 by Ray Bradbury
The Metamorphosis by Franz Kafka
The Diary of a Young Girl by Anne Frank
Nineteen Eighty-Four by George Orwell
questions.explanation: Ogawa read Anne Frank's diary as a teenager and has said it made her want to write. R hiding in a secret room echoes the annexe where the Frank family hid.

questions.stem: Reviewers often compare The Memory Police with Nineteen Eighty-Four. What do the two novels share?
options: A setting on a remote island cut off from the world
A narrator who is a member of the secret police
A state that controls what people may remember
A hero who leads a revolution that succeeds
questions.explanation: Both novels show power working through memory: what people are allowed to know about their past. Ogawa's version is quieter and stranger, with no explanation of who gives the orders.

questions.stem: How was the English translation recognised?
options: It won the Booker Prize and the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction
It won both the National Book Award and the International Booker Prize
It was banned in Japan until the English translation appeared
It was a finalist for the International Booker and National Book Award
questions.explanation: The translation was a finalist for the 2019 National Book Award for Translated Literature and the 2020 International Booker Prize.

questions.stem: Why should students be careful when quoting The Memory Police?
options: The narrator is unreliable, so any quotation from her must be untrue
Japanese idioms are left untranslated, so the meaning is often unclear
They are reading a translation, so the exact words are Stephen Snyder's
Ogawa revised the English edition, so it differs from the original novel
questions.explanation: In a translated text, word choice belongs partly to the translator. Analyse images and ideas with confidence, but be cautious about building an argument on a single English word.

questions.stem: What does the novel suggest about memory and identity?
options: Losing memories means losing parts of the self, until people vanish
Forgetting the past makes people happier and freer than before
Memory shapes what people own, but has little to do with who they are
Lost memories can be restored by seeing the lost objects once again
questions.explanation: As objects go, so do the feelings attached to them, and finally bodies and voices. The novel presents memory as what makes a person.

questions.stem: How does control work on the island?
options: The Memory Police pay islanders to report on their neighbours
The government explains each loss in public notices that islanders obey
Islanders carry out the losses themselves, burning their own things
The Memory Police destroy each object themselves while islanders watch
questions.explanation: The Memory Police enforce the rules, but most of the work is done by ordinary people getting rid of what they no longer remember. The novel suggests oppression depends on compliance.

questions.stem: What role does writing play in the novel?
options: It is one more thing the narrator gives up gladly once novels disappear
It is shown as pointless, since books are burned in the end anyway
It is a way of holding on to memory against the disappearances
It is the main tool the Memory Police use to control islanders
questions.explanation: R insists that the narrator keep writing even after novels vanish. Her manuscript becomes a way to preserve something, which makes writing itself an act of resistance.

questions.stem: What makes the dystopia of The Memory Police unusual?
options: The rulers' ideology is set out in detail in their speeches
Its oppression is driven by advanced surveillance technology
Loss is met with quiet acceptance rather than rebellion
Its hero leads a doomed rebellion against the island's rulers
questions.explanation: Many dystopias build towards a revolt. Here people adjust calmly to each loss, which is more disturbing because it feels so possible.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the first-person narration?
options: We see the island objectively, since the narrator remembers everything clearly
We see events as R does, sharing his clear memory of everything that is lost
We follow R's thoughts in his room, written up as a diary of his days
We experience forgetting from inside, through a narrator who cannot see the losses
questions.explanation: The narrator cannot describe what she has forgotten, so the reader feels the gaps with her. Her calm voice makes the losses seem normal, which is unsettling.

questions.stem: Most characters have no name, and the editor is known only as R. What is the effect?
options: It suggests the characters are based on real people Ogawa knew
It makes each character's history feel clear and individual
It gives the story the feel of a fable and suggests identity being worn away
It shows the novel is set in the far future, when names are no longer used
questions.explanation: Without names, the characters seem universal, as in a fable. It also fits a world where everything that makes people individual is slowly erased.

questions.stem: What does the secret room come to represent?
options: The narrator's wish to leave the island forever
The island's history before the disappearances
Memory kept safe, and also the cost of confinement
The Memory Police's power over the island's homes
questions.explanation: R's room preserves what the island has lost, but he can never leave it. The room is a refuge and a prison at once.

questions.stem: How would you describe the novel's tone?
options: Tense and fast-paced, like a thriller building to a daring escape
Bitter and satirical, openly mocking the island's rulers
Cold and technical, like a government report on the island
Calm, dreamlike and melancholy, even when terrible things happen
questions.explanation: Ogawa describes disappearances and raids in a quiet, gentle voice. The gap between the calm tone and the horror of events is a large part of the novel's power.

questions.stem: The translation often says that things 'were disappeared'. What is the effect of this phrasing?
options: It suggests that things simply wear out naturally over time
It suggests the islanders choose to make things disappear
It implies an outside force acts on things, hinting at hidden power
It reflects an error in translation that Snyder chose to keep
questions.explanation: 'Disappear' usually has no object. Using it as something done to things suggests someone is doing the disappearing, a usage that also recalls people 'disappeared' by real regimes.

questions.stem: Who says 'It doesn't hurt, and you won't even be particularly sad', and what does it show?
options: The old man, telling the narrator about the ferry's disappearance
An officer of the Memory Police, as he searches the father's study
The narrator's mother, explaining disappearances to her as a child
R, comforting the narrator when her own novels have disappeared
questions.explanation: The mother explains that disappearances are painless. That is what makes them dangerous: people do not grieve what they cannot feel, so they do not resist.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'In The Memory Police, forgetting is more frightening than force.' Discuss.
options: Ogawa suggests the island's quiet acceptance of loss is more chilling than the Memory Police's raids
The Memory Police is a novel by the Japanese writer Yoko Ogawa, translated into English by Stephen Snyder
This essay will discuss forgetting and force in the novel The Memory Police by Yoko Ogawa
In The Memory Police, the narrator hides her editor R in a secret room under her house
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and names what the paragraph will prove. The others retell, announce or state facts without making an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'When calendars disappear, it snows all the time.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: List the other objects that disappear before the calendars do
Retell what the narrator and R do on the snowy days that follow
Explain how the endless winter shows a society frozen without time
State that the snow is an important symbol in the novel
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the evidence suggests. Reading the snow as a symbol of a frozen, stalled society links the detail to the novel's ideas about memory and control.
